narrative.overview:
One performer, seven staged productions of the same script. The content (name, title, tagline, experience, skills, projects, blog) never changes; a switch in the header restages it in one of seven complete visual worlds: Avant-garde (the default), Engineer, Creative, Editorial, Arcade, Night Shift, and Metro. The system's personality is plural on purpose. Each world commits fully to its own register (the terminal, the studio, the dark gallery, the broadsheet, the arcade cabinet, the highway interchange at 3 a.m., the metro line). None of them is a theme laid over a neutral base, because the neutral base does not exist.

Underneath, one skeleton carries all seven: a fixed translucent header, a full-viewport hero, and a single centered column of sections (About, Experience, Education, Skills, Projects, Contact) at medium density. A world declares nine semantic color tokens (page, raised, text, secondary text, accent, accent hover, border, card, card hover), two font slots, and two radii, and the shared sections re-skin themselves. Only Hero, Experience, and Skills get a bespoke component per world; Metro alone adds a page-level overlay, the fixed line that indexes the sections.

The aesthetic philosophy is restraint everywhere except the accent and the display type. Every world has exactly one accent and spends it on small, high-signal things: buttons, period labels, rules, hover and selection states. Display typography carries identity. Motion is one shared reveal grammar (fade and rise on scroll, once) plus a single signature per world. Six signatures live in the hero; Metro's runs the length of the page, one scroll value driving the train marker, the station doors, and the rail.
keyCharacteristics: Seven complete worlds, one content source, switched at runtime and persisted per visitor.
One accent per world, spent on interactive and labeling elements only.
Display typography carries identity: monospace, geometric sans, heavy grotesk, display grotesk, slab poster, condensed signage, or black transit grotesk.
Flat, border-defined surfaces in six worlds; Creative alone lifts with shadow.
Shared reveal motion (fade, 30px rise, 0.5s, once) with a signature per world: six in the hero, Metro's along the whole scroll.

WebGL in two worlds (Avant-garde's particle field, Night Shift's interchange and its manifest vignettes), each mounted only while its world is active, held invisible until it has drawn, and backed by a CSS fallback or by nothing at all.
Scene materials stay in the scene: Arcade's candy and Night Shift's sodium, safety yellow, and steel never become UI chrome.
Bilingual by construction: every text node renders both locales and CSS shows one.

rules.name: The One Accent Rule
rules.body: Each world has exactly one accent and spends it on buttons, labels, rules, hover and selection states. Body copy, headings, and card surfaces never take the accent. Arcade's candy colors are surfaces with Cabinet Black text on them, never accents, and Night Shift's scene materials never leave the canvas.

rules.name: The Own Palette Rule
rules.body: A world uses only its own token set. No Candy Green in Engineer, no Creative shadow in Editorial, no Terminal Teal outside the terminal.

rules.name: The Dark Text on Bright Accent Rule
rules.body: Teal, Lime, and Gold are light accents, so filled buttons put the page color on them (11:1 to 16:1). Violet takes white (6.7:1). Signal Orange is the exception that needs care: it measures 3.0:1 on Newsprint and 3.3:1 under white text, so it lives on bold headings, rules, outlines, and uppercase button labels. Blue Spot takes Asphalt (5.4:1). Linha Verde is the one accent that takes white (4.6:1) and reads 4.3:1 on Enamel, so green text stays bold or uppercase.

rules.name: The Three Lights Rule
rules.body: Every Night Shift scene is lit by exactly three light families: Sodium overheads, one Blue Spot work light, and the traffic's own glow. Ambient stays at floor level (0.14 in the hero, 0.34 in a vignette) and nothing else emits.

rules.name: The Heading Slot Rule
rules.body: Headings never hardcode a family. They use the heading slot (`--font-heading`) so a world can swap the voice in one token.

rules.name: The Loud Display, Quiet Body Rule
rules.body: Identity lives in the display size and face. Body and label sizes stay between 0.75rem and 1.125rem in every world.

rules.name: The Sign Rule
rules.body: In Metro every heading is a sign: h1 through h3 sit at weight 900, and section titles are set white on Linha Verde. Green text elsewhere is bold or uppercase.

rules.name: The Same Bones Rule
rules.body: Section order, container widths, and the About, Education, Projects, and Contact structures stay shared by default. A world forks a section only when its identity needs it; today that is Hero, Experience, and Skills. Metro's line is an overlay on the page, not a section fork.

rules.name: The 896 Rule
rules.body: Section content lives in an 896px column. Only the header and the hero widen to 1152px.

rules.name: The Two-Radius Rule
rules.body: A world declares exactly two radii, `--radius-card` and `--radius-btn`. Chips, tags, and filters borrow the button radius; containers borrow the card radius. Night Shift's dock plate, chamfered by clip-path, and its square-cornered vignette bays are the recorded exceptions.

dos: Do declare a new world with the nine color tokens, two font slots, and two radii on its `[data-design]` selector, register it in `src/data/designs.ts`, and add it to the anti-FOUC allowlist.
Do keep the accent on buttons, labels, rules, and states (The One Accent Rule), and put the page color on light accents (11:1 to 16:1).
Do treat Signal Orange as a display color: bold headings, rules, outlines, and uppercase button labels. It measures 3.0:1 on Newsprint and 3.3:1 under white text.
Do resolve headings through the heading slot and body through the body slot; only Engineer's labels and the shared code face name JetBrains Mono directly.
Do render both locales in every text node behind `data-lang-show` so the language toggle never re-renders.
Do respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, and make new motion join the reveal grammar (fade, 30px rise, 0.5s, once).
Do keep bespoke sections to Hero, Experience, and Skills unless a world's identity needs another (The Same Bones Rule).
Do mount a WebGL scene only while its world is active, calibrate a lighter phone build, and ship a CSS fallback, as Avant-garde and Night Shift both do.
Do default `--arrival` to 1 in CSS and let `MetroLine` only ever raise it; a station once opened stays open, and the page reads fully without JavaScript.
Do light every Night Shift scene with its three families only: Sodium overheads, one Blue Spot work light, and the traffic's own glow (The Three Lights Rule).
donts: Don't mix tokens across worlds. No candy surface in Engineer, no Creative shadow in Editorial, no Terminal Teal outside Engineer (The Own Palette Rule).
Don't fork content per world. Copy, data, order, and links come from `src/data` and `src/i18n` only; a world may restage them, never rewrite or reorder them.

Don't let scene materials into UI chrome. Safety Yellow, Sodium, Tarmac, Steel, Concrete, Cardboard, Beam, and Packet Core exist inside the interchange and vignette canvases, the hero's fallback, and the arrival curtain; Blue Spot is Night Shift's only UI accent.
Don't add a greeting or eyebrow above the name in Night Shift or Metro; both open on the name itself, as an overhead road sign and as a platform sign.
Don't drive Metro from a second scroll source. The train, the doors, and the rail all read the one value `MetroLine` publishes.
